extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners studying peer review, conference organizers, and science-of-science scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how peer-review formats (single-blind vs double-blind) and review procedures (rating scales, anonymization practices) affect reviewer bias, reviewer disagreement, and the quality of editorial decisions at academic conferences. Uses empirical data from ICLR submissions and citation outcomes to assess effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige bias (author prestige effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may be biased by authors' prestige; double-blind peer review is hypothesized to reduce this 'prestige bias'. Author prestige was measured as the percentile of the mean author citations up to the year of submission (from MAG).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate by comparing mean reviewer scores and acceptance outcomes across prestige percentiles; use interaction terms between prestige and reviewing-format indicators in regressions; examine non-linear effects by grouping papers into prestige terciles. Note that effects can be heterogeneous across prestige levels (e.g., reduced scores for top-third authors but no significant boost for low/median prestige).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing quality / ability to identify low-quality papers (decision quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of decisions measured by post-decision citations: a less biased reviewing process should better differentiate low-quality papers from high-quality ones (e.g., rejected papers in a more meritocratic process should have lower subsequent citations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare 2-year citation distributions of rejected (and accepted when appropriate) papers across reviewing formats; control for confounds like changes in posting behavior that affect citation accrual; focus on rejected papers when accepted-paper citation comparisons are confounded by acceptance-related citation boosts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer disagreement (standard deviation among reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Masking authors' identities may remove easy heuristic cues and increase disagreement among reviewers; measured as the SD among the three reviewers' ratings for each paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare SD distributions across formats (e.g., single-blind vs double-blind); interpret increases in disagreement carefully — higher SD can reflect reduced use of biased heuristics rather than worse review quality. Use negative controls (years with same format) to check robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on acceptance decisions (translation of rating bias into outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reductions in rating bias (e.g., lower scores for prestigious authors) translate into differences in final acceptance depends on whether affected manuscripts are near the acceptance threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze acceptance rates and run regressions (e.g., linear probability models) interacting prestige with format or rating-scale changes. Consider the acceptance-rate regime: if acceptance is very high or very low, rating bias reductions may not change outcomes. Use matched year comparisons and statistical tests (Fisher's exact, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity effectiveness / deanonymization risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-blind review cannot achieve perfect anonymity: manuscript content and preprints can deanonymize authors; behavior such as posting on preprint servers before decisions affects anonymization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess anonymization quality by comparing papers posted before vs after decision date; consider that papers posted after decision date are more likely to remain anonymized and may show stronger double-blind effects. Treat posting timing as a moderator or stratify analyses by posting behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating-scale granularity effects (coarse vs fine rating scales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing rating scales (e.g., from 10-point to 4-point) may reduce reviewer bias by removing fine-grained ways to express subtle preferences for reputable authors or by changing perceptions of the top score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for interactions between scale-change indicators and prestige in regressions predicting acceptance; be cautious comparing mean ratings across different scales — use acceptance as the outcome when mean-rating scales are not comparable. Consider cognitive mechanisms and prior experimental evidence when interpreting effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige measurement method and matching accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Author prestige constructed as percentile of mean author citations up to submission year using Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG) author matches; matching strategy used email domain and field, with manual checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and report matching procedure and accuracy (reported ~78% in a 100-author random subsample). Evaluate sensitivity of results to matching errors and missing matches; consider robustness checks with alternative prestige measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating measurement: mean_score among reviewers and comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean_score is defined as the mean rating among the three reviewers for each paper; ICLR used a 10-point scale (2017-2019) and switched to a 4-point scale in 2020.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mean_rating when scales are comparable (same scale years). When scales change, avoid comparing raw mean ratings across scales; instead analyze acceptance or transform scores appropriately. Explicitly document reviewer count and aggregation rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of robust statistical methods, controls, and tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses employed OLS regressions with interaction terms, linear probability models for acceptance, nonparametric tests (Mann–Whitney U), Fisher's exact test, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, and robust standard errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for year effects (is_2018, is_2019, is_2020), use interaction terms to capture format-by-prestige effects, check linearity assumptions, and complement parametric models with nonparametric group comparisons and negative controls. Report R2, coefficients, SEs, t-stats, and p-values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonlinearity of bias across the prestige spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias effects may be nonlinear with respect to prestige; prior research suggests nonlinearity and the current study finds effects concentrated in the top-third prestige group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on linear models; perform nonparametric analyses such as tertile grouping and Mann–Whitney U tests across prestige bands. Report where effects concentrate (top, middle, bottom) and test for heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation-window and publication-date matching for quality measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality proxies based on citations require careful windowing: this study used 2-year citations from MAG and excluded papers published before Jan 1, 2016 or after Sep 30, 2018 to ensure at least two years of accumulation and reduce mismatches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match papers to publication records (use earliest publication date across venues), set clear inclusion windows for citation accumulation, and document matching success rates (e.g., 1368 of 1400 matched). Consider how posted time relative to decision affects citation comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample selection, temporal confounds, and submission-behavior changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy changes may alter submitter behavior and reviewer pools; e.g., after switching to double-blind, a much larger fraction of papers were posted after decision date, which can confound comparisons across years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check distributions of author prestige and acceptance rates across years (e.g., Kolmogorov–Smirnov, Fisher tests) to justify comparability. Acknowledge and test for behavioral shifts, and where possible use negative controls or stratified analyses. Prefer randomized trials when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential adverse effects on novelty and types of research
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-blind peer review might be harsher to novel work if reputable authors previously helped 'sell' risky/novel ideas; novel papers often experience delayed recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether double-blind review differentially affects novel papers by incorporating novelty indicators or long-term citation trajectories. Interpret short-term citation-based quality measures cautiously, and plan longer-window follow-ups (e.g., 10 years) where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definition of Acceptance for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance variable defined as binary =1 when the paper is not rejected (includes 'Accepted (oral)', 'Accepted (poster)', 'Invited to workshop' etc.), 0 when rejected; this was chosen to achieve a more balanced accepted vs rejected sample for power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state decision-category mappings and any year-to-year differences in categories. Recognize that changing definitions can affect comparability and statistical power; justify choices and test robustness to alternative acceptance definitions.
